snippet.title: Experience a Week in the Stone Age | Day 2: The Healer | Surviving Sickness 12,000 Years Ago
snippet.description:
A man is burning with fever, and the nearest hospital is twelve thousand years away. There are no doctors. No medicine cabinet. No word for "infection." There is only one woman — and everything she knows is stored inside her head.
Welcome to Day 2 of A Week in the Stone Age — a 7-part series following ordinary people through daily life 12,000 years ago, on the shores of a lake in what is now Yorkshire, England.
Today we follow the healer: a mother, gatherer, and keeper of a pharmacy that grows along the lake edge. The willow bark she boils this morning contains the same active compound as the aspirin in your bathroom cabinet — and she's using it eight thousand years before anyone will give it a name. By nightfall she'll break a fever, free a newborn who can't feed, and sit beside someone in the dark when there's nothing left to try.
In this episode:
→ Why willow bark was the original aspirin — and how she knew, without knowing the chemistry
→ The Stone Age tongue-tie procedure a paediatrician still performs today
→ How quarantine existed 11,000 years before anyone formalised it
→ Why these people were NOT primitive — they practised real, tested medicine
→ The chain of women, older than language, that carried this knowledge forward
→ Why the most important person in the camp tomorrow can't run, can't hunt, and remembers everything
📍 Based on real archaeological evidence from Star Carr, Yorkshire — the most important Mesolithic site in Britain (c. 9,300–8,480 BC)

snippet.title: Caesar's Disastrous Invasion Of Britain
snippet.description:
Today, we trace Julius Caesar’s dramatic invasions into Britain - two bold expeditions that tested Rome’s reach at the very edge of the known world. Ships were battered by storms, soldiers struggled with unfamiliar tides, and British warriors offered fierce resistance. Caesar never secured a lasting conquest of the island - so what drove him to try? Military necessity, retribution or a calculated move in his rivalry with figures like Pompey?

Joining us is historian and author Simon Elliott to unpack the politics, ambition and spectacle behind these campaigns, and to explore how these risky ventures helped shape the larger-than-life reputation that still defines Caesar today.

snippet.title: INVESTIGATING 12 Execution Methods Civilization Tried to ERASE | The Complete History
snippet.description:
Light your candle and draw the curtains. What I'm about to share exists between documented history and collective amnesia—twelve execution methods that once commanded the full machinery of empires, yet have vanished so completely their very existence strains belief.

I am Mr. Ravenhurst, and this is the complete investigation.

🕯️ THE 12 METHODS EXAMINED:

ANCIENT WORLD:
- Scaphism (The Boats) - Persia, 401 BC
- Poena Cullei (The Sack) - Rome, 100 BC - 1734 AD  
- The Brazen Bull - Ancient Sicily, ~560 BC

MEDIEVAL ERA:
- The Breaking Wheel - Last used Prussia, 1841
- Hanged, Drawn & Quartered - Last used England, 1820
- Execution by Elephant - Mughal India, documented 1817

EARLY MODERN:
- Pressing (Peine Forte et Dure) - Salem, 1692
- Gibbeting - Last used England, 1832
- Boiling Alive - Tudor England, 1531-1547

THRESHOLD OF MODERNITY:
- Lingchi (Death by a Thousand Cuts) - China, last photographed 1905
- Sawing - Medieval/Early Modern, fragmentary records
- Keelhauling - Dutch/British Navy, abolished 1720

📚 WHAT YOU'LL DISCOVER:

Every method in this investigation is verified through primary sources—court records, legal codes, eyewitness accounts, and in one case, actual photographs. I spent months in archives examining documents that chronicle the unthinkable. Some methods left archaeological evidence we can examine under laboratory lights. Others left only text, though text in legal codes carries its own weight of proof.

This is not legend. This is not folklore. This is documented history that civilization chose to forget.

⚖️ WHY THEY WERE FORGOTTEN:

These methods didn't disappear because they were exceptional—they disappeared because they were ordinary. They were the law. They were justice. Understanding why we forgot them reveals more about civilization than the methods themselves.

snippet.description:
Six hundred men sailed from Troy. One man survived. This is his story.

From double agents and deception networks to secret operations that fooled Hitler himself, this is the untold story behind the success of D-Day.

The workweek is over, the neighborhood is quiet, and there is an entire day ahead with no urgent schedule to follow. Long before smartphones and the internet, weekends unfolded at a slower pace, filled with familiar routines, simple pleasures, and moments shared with family and friends. Lawns are mowed, gardens are watered, family cars are carefully washed in the driveway, and neighbors pause for friendly conversations over white picket fences. snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Alderman (Black Death) | Day 5 of 7
snippet.description:
In November 1348, three of London's twenty-four aldermen were already dead. Two more were sick. The constables who walked the streets were dying. The clerks who kept the records were dying.

And somebody still had to run the city.

This is Day 5 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are the alderman of Vintry ward — a wine merchant turned city official who has spent nine years managing eight thousand people on the north bank of the Thames. You know every street, every landlord, every problem.

This morning your ledger has three complaints waiting. One of them is a landlord refusing to let the collection carts remove the bodies of his dead tenants. You walk there yourself. He tells you: what's the point — they're all going to die anyway. You tell him: the point is that we do the work while we can. The bodies are collected.

At noon you walk to the Guildhall. Eight empty chairs where aldermen used to sit. The Lord Mayor is still in his. The agenda: the burial ground is running over budget, seven ward constables are dead and need replacing, and the city's finances are collapsing because the port is emptying and the merchants are dying. Nobody has a solution. The meeting ends anyway.

This afternoon you sit in judgment in the ward court. A weaver hasn't paid his rent. Both his journeymen are dead. His apprentice ran home. He chose food over rent. The law says evict him. You grant him thirty days.

Your wife says it best, over supper: he's not wrong that they're all going to die. He's just wrong that it matters.

snippet.title: 1776: The Uncensored Story of The American Revolution
snippet.description:
Forget what you learned in school. Or from Hamilton. The American revolution was bigger and bloodier than you ever thought.

For the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, we bring you the undiscovered stories, heroes, and villains of the War for Independence. In this incredible six-part retelling, we go far beyond the 13 original colonies and the clash between American Patriots and British colonial troops. We traverse the Atlantic and plunge deep into the American West to discover a multi-front war that engulfed a diverse cast of characters – Indigenous people, enslaved Africans, American Loyalists, women of all social classes – and changed the face of world history.

EPISODE 1: UNLIKELY REVOLUTIONARIES 
We begin by profiling three unlikely revolutionaries: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and John Adams. 

EPISODE 2: REVOLUTION IN INDIAN COUNTRY 
When fighting breaks out between Britain and the American colonists, the native people of North America are forced to pick a side. 

EPISODE 3: THE SLAVES’ REVOLUTION
The American War for Independence was, in fact, two revolutions in one. There was the Revolution we know – of American Patriots against their British overlords. And there was the Revolution we don’t know – of enslaved Black people against their American overlords

snippet.title: D-Day: 100 Days For Freedom
snippet.description:
For the 82nd anniversary of the D-Day Landings, this documentary brings back to life the 100 days it took for the Allies to liberate Normandy, to break through the German line and to pave the way towards victory. 100 critical days, both heroic and tragic, that made history.

“The free men of the world are marching together to Victory!” These are the words of Commander Eisenhower to the Allied troops on June 6, 1944. A few hours later, they were around 150,000 to land on the Normandy coast. Operation “Overlord” was launched: one of the largest military operations of the 20th century. D-Day: 100 Days for Freedom propels us into the 100 sensational days that followed, while reviving the experiences of soldiers on both sides.

snippet.title: Modern Nightmare Entities: From Freddy Krueger to the Hat Man
snippet.description:
In the 1980s, young Cambodian refugees began dying in their sleep across 
Los Angeles. Healthy men with no medical history. No physical cause of death. 
Just terror frozen on their faces and families who knew exactly what had 
killed them: the nightmare demon.

A filmmaker named Wes Craven read about these deaths and created the most 
iconic modern nightmare entity: a burned figure with a razor glove who kills 
you in your dreams. But he wasn't inventing something new—he was translating 
an ancient phenomenon into contemporary horror cinema.

In 2009, a forum user posted doctored photographs of a tall, faceless figure 
in a suit. Everyone knew it was fiction. But then people started seeing him. 
In forests. In peripheral vision. Standing at the foot of their beds during 
sleep paralysis. Slenderman had somehow crossed from collaborative internet 
fiction into actual nightmares.

And now, millions of people are documenting the same entity: the Hat Man. 
Seven to eight feet tall. Wide-brimmed fedora. Standing motionless, radiating 
dread. Appearing during sleep paralysis across the world with disturbing 
consistency.

This is the complete history of modern nightmare entities—how horror cinema, 
internet culture, and viral phenomena transformed ancient sleep demons into 
the entities that haunt us today. And what neuroscience, psychology, and 
philosophy reveal about what these experiences actually are.

snippet.title: 7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London | 1348 Full Documentary
snippet.description:
7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London — the complete series in one full-length documentary.

In the autumn of 1348, the Black Death arrived in London. Within months it would kill between a third and a half of everyone in the city. This is the story of that catastrophe — not told through kings, battles, or cathedrals, but through seven ordinary people living one day at a time as the plague closed in around them.

snippet.title: Watching a City Burn: The Great Fire of London | AI Reconstruction

In September 1666, a small spark in a bakery on Pudding Lane changed the course of history forever. In just four days, the medieval city of London was reduced to ash, leaving 100,000 people homeless and destroying over 13,000 houses.

In this AI-enhanced reconstruction, we journey back to the 17th century to witness the chaos, the terror, and the eventual rebirth of a global metropolis. How did a single ember erase a city?
